meta.description: A free, friendly guide to quantum technology for Chicago students: how steel powered the South Side, and how the new quantum park at the old South Works site can open new careers.

hero.headlineFuture: Quantum can power its next chapter.
hero.subhead: The old South Works steel site is becoming a quantum technology park. Learn what that means, see the jobs it could bring, and find your place in it.
hero.trustNote: Free to use. No account needed, and we never ask for your real name.

timeline.title: Every revolution changed Chicago. Not everyone shared the gains.
timeline.intro: Here are five turning points. For each one, ask two questions: who gained, and who got left out?

stops.name: Railroads
stops.plain: Trains tied Chicago to the rest of the country.
stops.gained: Chicago became a huge railroad center with many jobs, and in 1937 the Pullman porters' union won the first major contract for a Black union.
stops.leftOut: Potawatomi and other Native nations were removed after an 1833 treaty, and Black Pullman porters (sleeping-car attendants) were kept in service jobs.

stops.name: Steel and heavy industry
stops.plain: Giant mills turned iron ore into steel.
stops.gained: Mills in South Chicago and nearby neighborhoods gave thousands of families steady work for about a century.
stops.leftOut: Many Black workers were passed over for promotions, yet steel paid for homes and college, and when the mills closed, whole neighborhoods lost those paychecks.

stops.name: The internet
stops.plain: Computers and phones got connected to each other.
stops.gained: Easy web browsers like Mosaic spread, and Chicago Connected later gave many CPS families free internet at home for learning.
stops.leftOut: Not everyone got online. In 2020, an estimated 100,000 Chicago students still lacked high-speed internet at home.

stops.name: Artificial intelligence (AI)
stops.plain: Software that learns patterns from examples.
stops.gained: Workers and companies that use AI tools gain new options, and a degree or more job training can help lower the risk of automation.
stops.leftOut: A Chicago Fed study of U.S. jobs found Black workers make up more than their share of 17 of the 30 jobs most likely to be automated (done by machines).

stops.name: Quantum technology
stops.plain: Computers built on the rules of very tiny things.
stops.gained: Illinois broke ground in September 2025 on a quantum technology park at the old South Works steel site, where steelmaking ended in 1992.
stops.leftOut: This time, jobs, training and a voice in the plan must reach neighbors in South Chicago. Planners say they are talking with City Colleges of Chicago about training and funding a neighborhood plan for South Chicago.

explainer.title: What is quantum, in 30 seconds?

steps.title: Bits
steps.text: Your phone and laptop store everything as bits. A bit is like a tiny switch that is either 0 or 1.

steps.title: Qubits
steps.text: A qubit is the quantum version of a bit. Until you measure it, it can be in a blend of 0 and 1. When you measure it, you always get a plain 0 or 1.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: Special programs can use that blend to help with a few hard problems, like studying how molecules behave.

explainer.notText: A quantum computer does not try every answer at once, and it will not replace your laptop. Today's machines are still small and make errors.

whyNow.jobsNote: Park planners list jobs like system operators, cryogenic plant technicians (people who run equipment kept at extreme cold), logistics workers and security staff. They say they are talking with colleges about training for all skill levels. Many of these jobs do not need a PhD.
